title: Crossover Stockton
description: Our current account of unmet needs in Stockton, what the evidence shows, and what we are doing.

chapters.title: See clearly. Act locally.
chapters.text: We’re finding out what’s happening in Stockton, where help is needed, and what can be done about it.
chapters.method: We gather public records, talk to people, visit places, and document what we learn and what happens when we try to help.

sections.title: About Crossover
sections.headline: How can post-scarcity technology solve real problems?
sections.text: We start with real needs in Stockton, take action, and use what we learn to discover what technology and human participation can make possible.

chapters.text: Dogs on Stockton’s streets need care, shelters are under pressure, and access to services can be difficult. We’re building a basic understanding of the problem.

chapters.title: Overview
chapters.summary: The need, the available care, and what remains unresolved.
chapters.teaser: The situation, what we know, and our current focus.

paragraphs.text: Dogs are being abandoned and found roaming Stockton's streets, but their circumstances vary. Some are lost or owned, and dogs living with people experiencing homelessness are not automatically abandoned. The number currently living on the streets remains unknown.

paragraphs.text: Stockton has an established network of care. Animal Services handles reports, sheltering, treatment, reunification, and adoption. Stockton Street Dogs provides street outreach and connects dogs with rescue and fostering. Veterinary providers, including Hard Luck, offer treatment, while St. Mary's provides services for people experiencing homelessness, including reported pet-inclusive housing at Pathways.

The central difficulty is getting dogs into the care they need. Animal Services reports recurring shelter-capacity pressure and appointment requirements for healthy strays. Affordable veterinary care is limited, rescue and foster resources depend on availability, and pet-inclusive housing has admission rules and capacity that we have not yet verified.

links.label: Animal Services reports recurring shelter-capacity pressure and appointment requirements for healthy strays
rescue and foster resources depend on availability

paragraphs.text: Efforts to improve care are underway. Stockton's animal shelter is being expanded, the City has authorized additional veterinary staffing and spay/neuter services, and Stockton Street Dogs is proposing a Canine Campus for overflow and recovery. Whether these efforts are increasing the number of dogs receiving care remains to be established.

links.label: Stockton's animal shelter is being expanded

paragraphs.text: We are examining how these pathways work in practice: what happens when someone reports a dog, which services can respond, where access breaks down, and what changes could help more dogs receive care.

chapters.title: What's happening in Stockton?
chapters.text: Published reports describe dogs being abandoned or roaming in Stockton, but they do not establish a current street-dog population or the circumstances of every dog seen outside.
chapters.imageAlt: Dog standing alone on a neighborhood sidewalk

sections.title: Abandoned and roaming dogs
sections.text: Local reporting describes abandoned and roaming dogs in several Stockton neighborhoods. Stockton Street Dogs reports more dumped-dog encounters than a year earlier, with particular concern in District 5. Those encounters are an attributed report, not a verified population estimate. Animal Services cautions that some roaming dogs are lost or owned; a sighting alone does not establish abandonment.

sections.title: Shelter capacity
sections.text: Stockton Animal Services reports that the municipal shelter is regularly at capacity. Its manager said sick, injured, and aggressive animals and confirmed abandonment cases receive priority, while healthy stray intake generally requires an appointment. A report of a dog does not guarantee immediate shelter entry.

sections.title: Veterinary access
sections.text: Local advocates and officials describe limited affordable, timely veterinary care and a sterilization backlog. The City approved extra spay/neuter services to address part of that pressure; completed procedures and the effect on access remain unverified.

sections.title: Placement and rescue
sections.text: Rescue groups, foster homes, adoption programs, and volunteers offer paths beyond immediate shelter intake. Animal Services described a temporary found-animal foster pathway, and Stockton Street Dogs maintains foster and adoption applications. Available spaces, eligibility, and outcomes vary and have not been measured here.

sections.title: Dogs living with people outside
sections.text: A dog living with an unhoused person is not automatically abandoned. Keeping people with their animals can involve food, veterinary care, and pet-accommodating shelter. A San Joaquin County survey found pet ownership among respondents, and a St. Mary's Pathways listing describes units for people with pets; current dog-specific access and availability have not been verified by Crossover.

chapters.title: What care is available?
chapters.text: These are documented care pathways, not a guarantee that a service has space, an appointment, or a response available today.

sections.title: Animal control and municipal sheltering
sections.text: Stockton Animal Services receives animal reports, responds to urgent cases, and operates the municipal shelter with intake, treatment, reunification, foster, adoption, and rescue coordination. City guidance directs nonemergency reports online and gives phone numbers for urgent animals and found-dog appointments. Healthy stray intake generally requires an appointment during reported capacity pressure.

sections.title: Street feeding and outreach
sections.text: Stockton Street Dogs reports feeding dogs and providing supplies during street outreach. Its public materials invite volunteers and rescue partners and describe foster and adoption pathways. These reports do not verify a current response to every request or a placement for every dog encountered.

sections.title: Veterinary care
sections.text: Hard Luck Animal Welfare Advocates provides veterinary and medical support connected to vulnerable and shelter animals, including work under a City agreement. The City also developed a Pet Wellness & Adoption Center with Hard Luck as a veterinary partner. Current appointment availability, eligibility, and additional treatment volume are not verified here.

sections.title: Foster care, rescue, and adoption
sections.text: Animal Services describes a temporary found-animal foster option and offers adoption and volunteer programs. Stockton Street Dogs links to foster and adoption applications and rescue partnerships. These pathways depend on suitable homes, volunteers, treatment, and available organizational capacity; a listing is not confirmation of an open place.

sections.title: Dogs living with unhoused people
sections.text: St. Mary's Community Services provides services for people experiencing homelessness, and a Pathways listing describes temporary housing units for people accompanied by pets. This may be an option for some people who need to remain with their animals, but current dog eligibility, occupancy, and admission rules have not been confirmed.

chapters.title: What's being done to improve care?
chapters.text: The efforts below are at different stages. A funded contract, completed building work, or proposal does not by itself establish more dogs receiving care.

sections.text: The City awarded a construction contract for shelter renovation and expansion, with planned treatment, isolation, rehabilitation, and public-access improvements. Crossover observed construction in October 2026.
Stockton Street Dogs proposes an additional campus for overflow sheltering, veterinary recovery, and care while dogs await placement.

The City approved a three-month Animal Balance agreement targeting approximately 200 spay/neuter procedures across three clinic events. This is a planned service quantity, not a completed-procedure count.

The City authorized four additional Hard Luck contract positions for veterinary and animal-care work. Authorization does not establish that the positions were filled or that treatment capacity increased.

chapters.title: What we're learning
chapters.headline: Understanding the Gap
chapters.text: Stockton has animal-control, shelter, veterinary, outreach, foster, and adoption pathways, but which services can respond to a particular dog is not always clear. Crossover is tracing where access may break down.
chapters.currentWork: Crossover received 7,183 Animal Services field-call case records on November 2, 2026, and began reviewing them on November 4. These are case records, not unique dogs, verified street sightings, or confirmed care outcomes.
chapters.nextStep: We are examining reporting and response pathways, contacting service providers, and preparing limited firsthand checks of reported conditions. The planned street observations have not yet been completed.

sections.title: Before the first field observation
sections.text: We plan to observe public areas near St. Mary's to learn what can be seen firsthand. No visit or street-dog count has been documented there yet. A report about the corridor is a lead, not proof of current conditions.

entries.narration: The planned observation is limited to public areas. Seeing no dogs would also be useful, and one visit could not establish a citywide count.
In the 2024 San Joaquin County Point-in-Time survey, 34 percent of respondents said they had a pet. That is not a Stockton-only measure or a count of street dogs.
A Pathways listing describes units for people accompanied by pets, but current access, dog eligibility, and outcomes remain unverified by us.

sections.title: What the field-call records may tell us
sections.text: Stockton Animal Services provided 7,183 field-call case records. We have begun reviewing them for report types, response patterns, and missing data. Cases are not unique animals, verified sightings, or outcomes.

entries.narration: The records arrived November 2, 2026, and the review began November 4.
The analysis remains in progress; we have not published a count of dogs currently living on Stockton's streets.
The separate 2024 figure of 3,106 stray-dog intake events covers the Animal Services service area. It must not be added to the field calls or treated as a street census.

sections.title: Reports of dumped dogs and a proposed response
sections.text: Stockton Street Dogs reports repeated dumped-dog encounters. We are treating its reported range as an attributed claim, not a verified count or rate for the city.

entries.narration: The group reported three to ten encounters a week in September 2026; the underlying cases and geography have not been independently checked.
Its Canine Campus is a proposal. It does not yet represent operating capacity or a measured outcome.

sections.title: What happened when we contacted Animal Services
sections.text: We visited Stockton Animal Services in October, submitted a volunteer application, and are following up on what happens next. One visit describes what we saw at that time; it does not establish shelterwide capacity or outcomes.

entries.narration: Our first visit documented a busy lobby, a posted instruction about dogs entering the building, and construction activity.
We submitted a volunteer application and have not yet documented an onboarding outcome.
The city awarded a 10.47 million dollar construction contract for shelter renovation. We have not verified additional capacity from completed work.

sections.title: Could every dog have a safe place?
sections.text: This is an exploratory question about care, human participation, and what future technology might make possible. It is not an announced Stockton program or a finding that AI or robotics can solve the problem.
sections.note: Editorial exploration: The Asher House offers one example of rescue, rehabilitation, rehoming, and lifelong sanctuary care. Its model raises questions about land, staffing, animal suitability, costs, and local partnerships that we have not answered.

entries.narration: We are examining the example as inspiration, not evidence that the same arrangement would work in Stockton.

sections.headline: From work to vocation.
sections.text: AI and robotics will replace many jobs. What if more of our lives could be spent caring for people, animals, and the world around us—rather than working simply to survive?

sections.headline: See clearly. Act locally.
sections.text: We show up, learn from people and evidence, take useful action, and make what we discover public.

sections.title: Starting with dogs
sections.text: Our first focus is street dogs and access to care. We're learning about the need, the help already available, and where access may be breaking down.
